country.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
country.tagline: Sun-baked Herzegovinian karst, mineral Žilavka and the 'empty barrel' Blatina, with monks still making wine at Tvrdoš.

stats.note: Officials reported 2,657 ha of wine grapes in the Federation of BiH in 2016 plus about 600 ha in Republika Srpska, and 177,400 hl of wine (as reported by Jancis Robinson); there is no vineyard register, so the figures are approximate.

country.overview:
Almost all of Bosnia and Herzegovina's wine comes from Herzegovina, the hot, stony south that drains to the Adriatic along the Neretva. Summers can hit 40 °C, the soils are thin karst and terra rossa, and the scenery around Mostar, Čitluk, Međugorje, Ljubuški, Stolac and Trebinje looks more like Dalmatia than central Europe. About 3,000 ha are planted, worked by up to 11,000 households, most of whom make wine for themselves; around 50 producers are registered and perhaps 30 sell commercially.

Two native grapes make up 60 to 65 percent of the vineyard. Žilavka is a firm, mineral, apricot-and-almond white, said to have been the preferred wine of the Austro-Hungarian emperors after 1878. Blatina is a dark, soft red whose flowers are functionally female, so it must be interplanted with a pollinator such as Trnjak, Vranac or Alicante Bouschet; its nickname 'empty barrel' comes from the poor yields of bad flowering years. Vranac grows around Trebinje, Plavac Mali near the Croatian border.

Viticulture here goes back to the Illyrians and Romans, survived four centuries of Ottoman rule (when wine was mostly made by Christian communities and monasteries), and grew under Austro-Hungarian administration from 1878. In the socialist era households were limited to 100 litres of wine a year, and large cooperatives such as Hepok in Mostar dominated. The 1990s war set the industry back badly; since then family estates (Vinarija Čitluk, Podrumi Andrija, Vukoje, Tvrdoš, Nuić, Škegro, Brkić, Carski Vinogradi) have rebuilt it, and the Herzegovina Wine Route, opened in 2007, was relaunched in 2023. The country imports about five times more wine than it exports.

history.title: Vines in Roman Dalmatia
history.text: Herzegovina lay in the Roman province of Dalmatia; local tradition and archaeology link viticulture to the Illyrians and Romans more than 2,000 years ago.

history.title: Tvrdoš monastery cellar
history.text: The Serbian Orthodox monastery of Tvrdoš near Trebinje, founded in the late 15th or early 16th century, has a wine cellar dating to the 15th century; its monks still make Vranac and Žilavka.

history.title: Austro-Hungarian Herzegovina
history.text: Austro-Hungarian administration modernised viticulture around Mostar; Žilavka became a favourite at the imperial court, and land at Trebinje was part of Emperor Franz Joseph's personal vineyard.

history.title: War and the Wine Route
history.text: The war devastated vineyards and wineries; the Herzegovina Wine Route opened in 2007 and was relaunched in 2023.

country.classification: Bosnia and Herzegovina is not in the EU, and no wine names from it appear in the EU or UK geographical-indication registers. Wine law is set separately by the two entities (the Federation and Republika Srpska), and the traditional names Mostarska Žilavka and Mostarska Blatina are widely used on labels. A national vineyard register did not exist as of the last available reporting, so origin rules are loosely enforced.
country.climate_soils: Herzegovina has a Mediterranean-influenced climate with very hot, dry summers, mild winters and high sunshine; soils are karst limestone with pockets of terra rossa and stony alluvium along the Neretva. Northern Bosnia is continental and has only scattered vineyards.

grapes.name: Žilavka
grapes.note: Native white of Herzegovina: firm, mineral, apricot and almond; the country's signature wine.

grapes.name: Blatina
grapes.note: Native red with female flowers that needs a pollinator; soft, dark-fruited; nicknamed 'empty barrel'.

grapes.name: Vranac
grapes.note: Montenegrin red grown around Trebinje and in eastern Herzegovina.

grapes.name: Trnjak
grapes.note: Local red often interplanted with Blatina.

sources.title: Jancis Robinson: Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the crossroads
Decanter: Herzegovina, a wine lover's guide

regions.name: Herzegovina
regions.tagline: The Neretva's hot karst country: Žilavka, Blatina and monks' Vranac.
regions.summary: Herzegovina, the southern part of the country, holds nearly all the vineyards: around Mostar and the Neretva valley, Čitluk (with Međugorje), Ljubuški, Stolac and Čapljina in the west, and Trebinje in the south-east near Dubrovnik. Čitluk is the largest wine municipality and home of Vinarija Čitluk and Podrumi Andrija; Trebinje's Tvrdoš monastery and Vukoje estate make the region's best-known Vranac.
regions.history: Austro-Hungarian rule from 1878 brought viticultural schools and a market in Vienna; under socialism the Hepok cooperative dominated; the 1990s war broke the industry, and family wineries rebuilt it.
regions.terroir: Karst limestone, terra rossa and stony alluvium; summers up to 40 °C; dry and windy.
regions.grapes: Žilavka, Blatina, Trnjak, Vranac, Plavac Mali, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay.
regions.classification: Traditional names Mostarska Žilavka and Mostarska Blatina; no EU-recognised GIs.

sources.title: Jancis Robinson: Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the crossroads
Decanter: Herzegovina, a wine lover's guide

sites.name: Tvrdoš Monastery winery
sites.text: The Serbian Orthodox monastery of Tvrdoš on the Trebišnjica near Trebinje dates from the late 15th or early 16th century. One of its wine cellars is from the 15th century, and the monks still make Vranac and a flinty Žilavka, with a monk as cellar master.

sites.name: Vukoje, Trebinje
sites.text: Radovan Vukoje harvested his first grapes in 2000 and built one of Herzegovina's largest private wineries near Trebinje, on land that was once part of Emperor Franz Joseph's personal vineyard. Its pure Vranac and Žilavka are benchmarks.

sites.name: Podrumi Andrija, Paoča (Čitluk)
sites.text: The Ćorić family's winery at Paoča near Čitluk made Žilavka for Tito under special permission in the socialist era and kept working through the 1990s war. Its Blatina Andrija Selection is a reference for the grape.

sites.name: Vinarija Čitluk
sites.text: Čitluk is Herzegovina's largest wine municipality, and Vinarija Čitluk its biggest producer. Its Žilavka and Blatina come from the stony Brotnjo plateau, which includes the pilgrimage village of Međugorje.

sites.name: Mostar
sites.text: Mostar, with its rebuilt Old Bridge (UNESCO), is the regional capital and starting point of the Herzegovina Wine Route. The Mostarska Žilavka and Mostarska Blatina names come from the vineyards around it.
